newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economic data breathes life into EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: German economic data breathes life into EMU hopes.

text.p: Stronger-than-expected German economic statistics are bolstering hopes that Bonn might find a way to trim its budget deficit and meet the criteria for joining European economic and monetary union.

Economists said that various reports in the last two days, including unemployment, industrial output and orders and gross domestic product (GDP) data, should dampen mounting scepticism about German participation in EMU.
"The growth outlook has improved," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers. "The government should find a way to come close to EMU targets."
Earlier this week, doubts about Germany's ability to qualify for EMU appeared to be growing with several Bundesbank council members openly expressing scepticism.
But that was before the new data raised hopes that the economy might yet revive enough to create jobs and increase tax revenues, allowing a cut in the budget deficit.

Although no one is lifting their forecast yet, some economists believe that Germany still has a chance of achieving the government's 2.5 percent economic growth target -- a level it sees as crucial to being ready to qualify for EMU.
"The data have allowed the government to retain hope of a recovery," said Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs.
Most analysts still expect Germany to fall short of strictly meeting the three percent deficit to economic output target stipulated by the Maastricht treaty.
But they say Bonn may yet come close enough to allow last-minute accounting procedures to help it sneak under that level.
"We see Germany's budget deficit at 3.2 percent in 1997 but we expect Germany will still be able to join European monetary union," said Frank Schroeder, analyst at Trinkaus & Burkhardt.
Over the last two days, Germany has been able report figures for industrial output and production showing signs of stronger growth.
Flat economic growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 exceeded expectations of a small decline and February's unemployment increase was smaller than expected.

Economists said that cutting Germany's jobless total is the key to making the EMU grade. If Germany were able to find jobs for 100,000 of the 4.316 million that were out of work in February, the government could save around four billion marks ($2.3 billion), one said.
Although the country faces huge structural problems which limit job growth, at least some expect joblessness to decline from this summer.

"Based on the forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth in the government's annual economic report, I believe we will see a fall in the seasonally adjusted unemployment figure at the middle of the year," said Hans-Peter Leikeb, head of the Federal Labour Office's jobs market research wing.

According to Mayer at Goldman, that should enable Germany to trim its budget deficit to 3.4 percent of gross domestic product -- a level still well above the three percent target that Finance Minister Theo Waigel has promised that Germany will meet this year.
But it will be close enough for Waigel to juggle the nation's books in such a way as to bring the deficit down to the magic three percent mark.
"We are seeing the emphasis shift from a liberal interpretation of the Maastricht treaty to a liberal interpretation of accounting methods," Mayer said.

Economists believe that through a number of measures such as delaying a cut in the solidary surcharge tax, cutting social benefits and implementing a government spending freeze, Germany will be able to chop several tenths of a percentage point off its deficit and meet the three percent level.
"Germany should in the end come close to the three percent target," Nerb said. "The government will be on the safe side and take what measures are needed." ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
